summary: Defines bindings and a BIND method for WebDAV, so that multiple URIs can be mapped to the same resource. Servers must keep the integrity of any bindings they allow. It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: One file gets several names, like a person with a nickname, and all names lead to the same thing.

questions: how to create multiple names for the same resource
subtitle: Create multiple names for the same file, like aliases in a filesystem.

tldr.problem: WebDAV resources sit in hierarchies where a single resource can belong to only one collection, but sometimes a resource needs to be accessible from multiple locations without copying it.
tldr.mechanism: The BIND method lets clients create additional URI mappings to existing resources. UNBIND removes bindings, and REBIND moves them atomically. Two new properties track resource identity and all its bindings.
tldr.outcome: Resources can appear in multiple collections, but servers must maintain binding integrity and detect problematic loops. New status codes handle these cases.

today: RFC 5842 is an Experimental specification that has not been adopted as an Internet Standard. It extends WebDAV to support multiple bindings, a feature some implementations support but which remains optional in the WebDAV ecosystem.

sections.title: The Problem of Single Locations
sections.content:
WebDAV resources live in a hierarchy of collections, like files in folders. Normally, a resource belongs in exactly one place. But what if a photograph of a bird should appear in both a "birds" folder and a "nature" folder without being duplicated? What if a shared document used by multiple departments needs to be accessible from each department's folder? Copying the resource wastes storage and breaks synchronization when it changes. The BIND method solves this by letting clients create alternative URIs that point to the same resource.

This specification defines how bindings work, introduces three new methods (BIND, UNBIND, REBIND), and adds properties to track which bindings exist and to prove that two URIs reference the same underlying resource.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a file belongs in multiple categories. Instead of copying it, you make new names for it. BIND creates a new name, UNBIND removes a name, and REBIND moves a name.

sections.title: Bindings and URI Mappings
sections.content:
A binding is a relation between a path segment (like foo.html) and a resource. Bindings are part of a collection's state. When you create a binding from foo.html to a resource R in collection C at http://example.com/CollX/, clients can now access R using the URI http://example.com/CollX/foo.html.

This creates a URI mapping. If the same collection is accessible via multiple URIs (for example, /CollX/ and /CollY/ both point to the same collection due to a prior binding), then a single resource can be reached through multiple URIs: /CollX/foo.html and /CollY/foo.html both access resource R.

Binding loops can occur: if a collection C creates a binding to itself, an infinite number of URIs map to C. Servers must detect loops during operations with Depth: infinity, such as PROPFIND traversing a tree.
sections.eli5: A binding is a connection between a name and a resource. Creating a binding gives the resource a new name you can use. If that name is in a collection with multiple paths to it, the resource gets even more names.

sections.title: BIND, UNBIND, and REBIND Methods
sections.content:
The BIND method creates a new binding from a path segment to an existing resource. The request targets a collection and provides the segment name and the resource URI. On success, the server returns 201 (Created) if a new binding was created or 200/204 if an existing binding was replaced. Preconditions ensure the resource exists, supports bindings, and a cross-server binding is permitted if needed.

The UNBIND method removes a specific binding from a collection. It does not delete the resource; if other bindings exist, the resource remains accessible through them. The request provides the segment to remove. Preconditions ensure the binding exists and is not write-locked.

The REBIND method atomically removes a binding from one location and adds it to another, like an atomic move. It takes the segment for the new name and the URI of the old binding to remove. This is safer than separate UNBIND and BIND operations.

Existing WebDAV methods (COPY, MOVE, DELETE) are updated to respect bindings: DELETE removes only the one binding addressed, COPY preserves bindings to destination, and MOVE is compatible with multiple bindings.
sections.eli5: BIND creates a new name for a resource. UNBIND removes a name (but not the resource). REBIND moves a name from one place to another as a single operation.

sections.title: Properties for Tracking Resources and Bindings
sections.content:
Two new properties support bindings:

DAV:resource-id is a required property that uniquely identifies a resource across all time. It can be a URI using the urn:uuid scheme or another globally unique format. All requests to different URIs pointing to the same resource return the same resource-id, allowing clients to confirm they are working with the same underlying resource even when accessed through different names.

DAV:parent-set is an optional property that lists all bindings to a resource. It contains href and segment pairs, one for each collection holding a binding to the resource. This lets clients discover all ways to reach a resource. However, maintaining parent-set is costly and reveals directory structure, so servers may omit it.
sections.eli5: Resource-id is like a permanent ID number for a file, so you know two different names point to the same file. Parent-set is a list of all the names and places where you can find the file.

sections.title: Handling Loops and Reporting Status
sections.content:
Two new HTTP status codes handle binding scenarios:

208 Already Reported is used in PROPFIND responses when a collection with multiple bindings is traversed with Depth: infinity. The first binding to a collection returns 200 (OK) with full details; subsequent bindings return 208 with no response body, avoiding redundant information. Clients must explicitly request this code by signaling support with a DAV request header.

508 Loop Detected indicates that a Depth: infinity request encountered a binding loop and terminated. This is returned when a client does not support 208, or when an operation cannot be completed despite the loop.

Servers MAY reject CREATE requests that would create loops (set by the DAV:cycle-allowed precondition). This is optional; servers supporting cycles can use both status codes together.
sections.eli5: When asking for information about a file with multiple names, 208 means "I already told you about this one." 508 Loop Detected means "there's a circular loop and I stopped."
